Part I
Getting Started
Chapter 1

Welcome to WEBcreator

WEBcreator is a website design program: a tool for arranging text, pictures, shapes, navigation bars, forms and media on a page exactly where you want them, and then publishing the result as a real, working website. It belongs to the just a… family of apps and works in the tradition of Serif's WebPlus — the same ideas, the same menus, in the same places.

What a website designer is

A word processor pours text down a page. A website designer is different: the page is a canvas, and everything on it — a logo, a headline, a block of text, a photo, a navigation bar, a button, a contact form — is a separate object you position freely. You design the page by eye, and the program writes the HTML and CSS for you behind the scenes.

If you have used Wix, Squarespace or Serif's WebPlus, you already know the idea. The one thing to unlearn, if you have only used a word processor, is this: you no longer type down a page — you place things on it, and the finished page is a website, not a printout.

The object model

Everything you put on a page is an object. There are the familiar layout objects — text frames, artistic text, pictures, shapes and lines, tables — and then the web objects that make a page a living site:

  • Navigation bars that list your pages automatically;
  • Buttons that link somewhere;
  • Forms for enquiries, and search boxes;
  • Share buttons for social media;
  • Photo galleries, YouTube and Vimeo video, audio players and Google Maps;
  • a News Feed that builds itself from your pages;
  • HTML fragments and custom CSS for anything bespoke.

Because they are all objects, the skills are shared: whatever the kind, you select it, move it, resize it, colour it, align it and layer it in exactly the same way. Learn those moves once and they apply everywhere.

The just a… family

WEBcreator has three companions, built to work together:

  • PAGEdesigner makes printed documents — flyers, newsletters, booklets — the same way WEBcreator makes websites;
  • PAINTcanvas is the image editor — WEBcreator hands a photo to it for retouching and gets the result straight back;
  • DRAWmaster is for vector illustration and logos.

They share the CREATORsuite launcher and a common Documents/just a… folder, so your work is easy to find. Once you know one app, the others feel familiar.

About this guide

This User Guide is the complete reference. It is organised in parts: the first gets you working, the middle teaches each skill in depth with step-by-step procedures, then come the web objects and site-wide features, worked projects you can follow start to finish, publishing, and finally a reference section — menus, shortcuts, a catalogue of templates and shapes, a glossary and troubleshooting.

NoteThroughout, a numbered “To …” box is a procedure you can follow exactly. A Tip suggests a faster or better way. A Remember box flags something easy to forget.

For a gentler first read, start with the Quick Start Guide (Help ▸ Quick Start), which takes you from a blank page to a published site in about a dozen short steps.

Conventions used here

A few conventions keep the instructions short:

  • Menu ▸ Command means “open this menu and choose this command”, e.g. File ▸ Publish….
  • Keys are shown like Ctrl+S; on a Mac read Ctrl as Cmd.
  • Click means the left mouse button; right-click opens a context menu; double-click opens whatever the object is for (its editor dialog, or edit-in-place for text).
  • Drag means press, move, release.
Chapter 2

Starting Out

This chapter covers the very first things: launching the program, the Startup Assistant that greets you, and the three ways to begin a site — from a ready-made design, from a blank page, or by opening work you already have.

Launching the program

Open just a… WEBcreator from the CREATORsuite launcher, from your system's application menu, or by running webcreator in a terminal. The first time it opens it may take a moment to settle; after that it starts quickly.

The Startup Assistant

Each time it launches, WEBcreator shows the Startup Assistant — your hub for beginning work. Down its left side are three sections: Use Design Template, Start New Site and Open Saved Site.

To begin from the Startup Assistant

  1. Choose Use Design Template to start from a ready-made design (see the next chapter),
  2. or Start New Site to begin with a blank page of a chosen width,
  3. or Open Saved Site to reopen recent work or browse for a saved file.
  4. Make your choice and the Assistant closes, leaving your new site open.
TipPrefer to start straight on a blank page? Untick Show the Startup Assistant when the app opens at the bottom. You can always begin a new site from File ▸ New Site.

Starting a blank site

Choose Start New Site to begin with an empty page.

To start a blank site

  1. In Start New Site, give the site a name.
  2. Choose a page width in pixels (960 suits most sites; 1000 or 1200 give a wider canvas).
  3. Pick a column layout — full width, two columns or three — to lay guide frames you can drop content into.
  4. Decide on Responsive (see below), then click Create Site.
NoteA website page has a fixed width but grows as tall as its content — you drag the page’s bottom edge to make it longer, so there is no fixed “paper size” as there would be in a print program.

Fixed-width or responsive

A website can be laid out two ways, and you choose which at the start (and again when you publish):

  • Static (fixed width) — the classic approach. The page is exactly as wide as you designed it; on a narrow phone the visitor pinches and scrolls. Simple and predictable, and best when most of your visitors are on a desktop.
  • Responsive — the whole design scales down to fit any screen, so a visitor on a phone sees the full layout shrunk to fit without side-scrolling. This is the modern default for a site that will be read on phones and tablets.
TipNot sure? Leave it static while you design, then turn Responsive on at Publish time and preview it on a phone — you can switch back and forth freely.

Opening and saving

WEBcreator sites are saved with a .webc extension.

To save your work

  1. Choose File ▸ Save or press Ctrl+S.
  2. The first time, give the site a name. It is saved into your shared Documents/just a… folder by default, so the launcher can find it.
  3. Use File ▸ Save As… to keep a separate copy under a new name.

To open an existing site

  1. Choose File ▸ Open and browse to a .webc file, or
  2. pick a recent file from File ▸ Open Recent, or from the Open Saved Site page of the Startup Assistant.

WEBcreator also opens work from the program it stands in for and from the web at large: File ▸ Open WebPlus Site… reads a Serif WebPlus .wpp publication, and from the Startup Assistant's Import… menu you can import a whole website folder, or a single web page from its URL, each as an editable site.

Chapter 3

The Workspace

Everything you do happens in the workspace: your page in the middle, the tools down the left, the menus and toolbars along the top, and the panels on the right. This chapter names every part so the rest of the guide can refer to them.

A tour of the window

A new site opens with the page centred and everything you need arranged around it.

The parts are:

  • the menu bar and toolbars across the top;
  • the tool palette down the left edge;
  • the rulers framing the page;
  • the page itself in the centre;
  • the tabbed panels on the right;
  • the status bar along the bottom, where a hint explains the current tool.

The tool palette

The vertical tool palette on the left holds the tools you draw and edit with. It is longer than a print program's, because a website has more kinds of object.

From the top: the Pointer (select and move), the Hand and Zoom tools for getting around, then the object tools grouped by kind — Artistic Text and Creative Frame Text; Table; Picture, Lightbox Image and Photo Gallery; Rectangle, Ellipse and Line; then the web objects: Navigation Bar, Button, Form, Search Box, Share Buttons, HTML Code, YouTube, Vimeo, Audio, Google Map and News Feed. Click a tool, then drag on the page to place it; its name and a hint appear in the status bar.

TipPress Esc or click the Pointer at any time to stop drawing and go back to selecting.

Menus and toolbars

The menu bar gathers every command under File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Arrange, then the Preview, Publish and SEO items and Help. The complete menu reference is Appendix A.

Below the menus, the Standard toolbar carries the everyday buttons and a View HTML toggle that reveals the page's source. An Insert toolbar sits alongside it with Site Structure and the alignment buttons, and an Apps toolbar links across to PAINTcanvas and PAGEdesigner.

The panels

The tabbed panels on the right are where you inspect and fine-tune whatever is selected — the Site / Pages structure, Transform, Colour, Swatches and Layers. The Site panel is the heart of a multi-page site: it shows every page as a tree you can add to, rename and reorder.

TipThe Site Structure button on the Insert toolbar brings the Site / Pages panel to the front whenever you need to jump between pages or rearrange them.

Moving around and zooming

You will zoom in to place things precisely and out to judge the whole page.

To change the zoom

  1. Hold Ctrl and scroll the mouse wheel, or
  2. choose View ▸ Zoom In / Zoom Out, or
  3. use View ▸ Actual Size and Fit Page Width to jump to 100% or to frame the full width.

The Hand tool — or holding the space bar and dragging — slides the page around when you are zoomed in.

Rulers, grid and snapping

The rulers along the top and left show position in pixels. From the View menu you can toggle the rulers, a background grid, snap to grid and a crosshair that follows the cursor. Snapping, and the gentle pull objects give off as you drag past each other's edges and centres, is how you keep columns, rows and margins lined up without measuring.

Part II
Core Skills
Chapter 4

Working with Objects

Text frames, pictures, shapes, buttons, forms and galleries are all objects, and they are handled the same way. Master the moves in this chapter — select, move, size, rotate, align, order, group, lock — and they serve you everywhere in the program.

Placing an object

To place any object

  1. Click its tool in the palette (or choose it from the Insert menu).
  2. Drag a box on the page where you want it. For web objects such as a picture, gallery or map, an editor opens so you can set it up.
  3. Switch to the Pointer to move or resize it.
NoteInsert ▸ … drops a default-sized object in the centre of the page if you would rather not drag out its size by hand.

Selecting objects

To select objects

  1. Choose the Pointer tool.
  2. Click an object to select it — a frame of handles appears around it.
  3. Hold Shift and click more objects to add them to the selection.
  4. Or drag a box across empty space to select everything it touches.
  5. Press Esc (or click empty space) to deselect; Ctrl+A selects everything on the page.

Moving and resizing

With one or more objects selected:

  • Move — drag any selected object; the whole selection moves together.
  • Resize — drag a corner or edge handle. Dragging a corner keeps a picture's proportions.
  • Nudge — tap the arrow keys to move a small, exact step at a time.
  • Rotate — drag the round handle above the object, or use the Rotate tool.
TipGuides, the grid and other objects give off a gentle snap as you drag past their edges and centres — let it do the aligning for you.

The Transform panel

When “close enough” is not enough, the Transform panel (and Arrange ▸ Transform…) lets you type exact numbers.

To place an object precisely

  1. Select the object.
  2. Open Transform and type its X and Y position, its width and height, or a rotation angle.
  3. Press Enter. This is the reliable way to make two objects exactly the same size, or to sit something a precise distance from the edge.

Aligning and distributing

Alignment is what turns a rough arrangement into a crisp one. Select two or more objects, then use Arrange ▸ Align:

  • Left / Centre / Right edges line up their vertical edges or centres;
  • Top / Middle / Bottom edges line up their horizontal edges or centres;
  • Centre on Page Horizontally centres the selection across the page.

A row of buttons, a grid of photos, a stack of headings — all look intentional once aligned. The alignment buttons are also on the Insert toolbar for one-click access.

Order, grouping and locking

Objects stack in the order you create them, newest on top. Use Arrange to change that:

  • Bring to Front / Send to Back, and Forward One / Back One, so a caption can sit over a photo;
  • Lock / Unlock (Ctrl+L) pins something so you cannot nudge it by accident.
RememberA locked object cannot be dragged — that is the point. Unlock it from Arrange ▸ Lock / Unlock when you need to move it again.

Cut, copy, paste and duplicate

The usual editing commands all apply to objects:

  • Ctrl+X / Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V cut, copy and paste;
  • Duplicate (Ctrl+D) drops a copy a little offset from the original;
  • Ctrl+Z undoes and redo steps forward again — there is a deep undo history, so experiment freely.
TipCopying an object and pasting it onto another page is the simplest way to reuse something you have built — a styled heading, a logo, a coloured panel.
Chapter 5

Text

Text is the heart of most pages. WEBcreator handles it the WebPlus way: body copy lives in frames you can link and flow, headlines are artistic text you scale freely, and it all publishes as real, selectable, searchable web text — never as a picture of words.

Frame text

To add a block of body text

  1. Choose the Creative Frame Text tool.
  2. Drag a rectangle on the page — that is a text frame.
  3. Type, or paste; the text wraps inside the frame’s edges automatically.
  4. Switch to the Pointer to move or resize the frame; the text re-wraps to fit.

Artistic text

Where frame text is for paragraphs, artistic text is a single line you can scale to any size — the tool for mastheads, titles and pull-quotes. Choose the Artistic Text tool, click, and type; then drag a corner handle to make it as large as you like. It publishes as ordinary styled web text, so it stays sharp at any size and a search engine can still read it.

Fonts, size, colour and alignment

Select some text — a word, a line or a whole frame — and set its look from the Format menu and the text controls:

  • Font and size;
  • Bold (Ctrl+B), Italic (Ctrl+I) and Underline (Ctrl+U);
  • Colour, from the Colour panel;
  • Alignment — left, centred, right or justified;
  • Line spacing, to open a dense block up or draw a loose one in.
NoteWEBcreator embeds the fonts it needs when it publishes, so a visitor sees the typeface you chose even if they do not have it installed.

Lists

To turn paragraphs into a bulleted or numbered list

  1. Select the paragraphs.
  2. Choose a style from Format ▸ Lists / Bullets — a disc, circle or square bullet, or 1-2-3, a-b-c or i-ii-iii numbering.
  3. The list indents neatly; a numbered list renumbers itself if you add or remove an item. Remove list turns it back into plain paragraphs.

Hyperlinks in text

Any word or phrase can become a link.

To make text into a link

  1. Select the words you want to turn into a link.
  2. Choose Insert ▸ Hyperlink….
  3. Choose where it goes — another page in your site, a web address, an email, or an anchor further down the page — and click OK.
  4. The linked words take on the site’s link colour; test them in Preview.

Links are covered in full in the Navigation, Links & Site Structure chapter.

Importing text, and spell check

Insert ▸ Import Text… pours a long text file straight into a frame, so you can draft in a word processor and lay it out here. Before you publish, check the spelling:

To check spelling across the whole site

  1. Choose Format ▸ Check Spelling… or press F7.
  2. WEBcreator scans the text on every page and lists any word it does not recognise.
  3. For each one, choose a suggestion and Change All, Ignore it, or Add to Dictionary.
NoteThe first time you use it, WEBcreator offers to download a small English dictionary (about 4 MB, once).
Chapter 6

Pictures and Galleries

Pictures bring a page to life. WEBcreator keeps them in frames you can crop and style, turns one into a click-to-enlarge lightbox, strings several into a gallery, and hands off to PAINTcanvas when a photo needs real editing.

Picture frames

To place a photograph

  1. Choose the Picture tool and drag a box — a picture frame.
  2. Choose an image file when prompted (or double-click an empty frame later).
  3. The picture fills the frame. Design the layout first with empty frames and drop the photos in later — a frame can wait.
NoteKeeping images in frames (rather than loose on the page) lets you resize the hole and the picture independently, and swap one photo for another without disturbing the layout. WEBcreator copies each picture into the site, so publishing gathers everything it needs.

Fitting, cropping and borders

A picture either fills its frame (cropping to the edges) or sits inside it. To show only part of a photo, use the Crop tool:

To crop a picture

  1. Select the picture and choose the Crop tool (or double-click to open Crop Picture).
  2. Drag the handles inward to hide the parts you do not want.
  3. Switch back to the Pointer. The hidden area is kept, so you can re-crop later.

Round the frame's corners or give it an outline from the panels to finish it off.

Lightbox images

A Lightbox Image is a thumbnail that, when a visitor clicks it, opens the full-size picture in a dark overlay over the page — the familiar way to show a gallery of photos without sending the visitor to another page. Place it like any picture, and set its small (thumbnail) and large (full) images.

Photo galleries

A Photo Gallery shows a series of pictures in turn, fading from one to the next — perfect for a hero banner or a portfolio strip.

To build a photo gallery

  1. Choose the Photo Gallery tool and drag out its size.
  2. In the Photo Gallery editor, add the pictures it should show and put them in order.
  3. Set the interval between slides and the fade time, and how each picture should fit its frame.
  4. Click OK. The gallery cycles automatically on the published page.

Editing a photo in PAINTcanvas

When a photo needs more than cropping — brightening, retouching, removing a background — WEBcreator sends it to its sister app.

To edit a picture in PAINTcanvas

  1. Select the picture.
  2. Click Edit in PAINTcanvas on the Apps toolbar.
  3. Make your edits in PAINTcanvas and save. The edited version comes straight back into your page, in place.
TipNo photo to hand? Create an image with AI can generate one from a short description, dropped straight into the selected frame.
Chapter 7

Shapes, Lines and QuickShapes

Shapes and lines give a page structure and emphasis — a coloured band behind a header, a rule between sections, a star on an offer. WEBcreator's QuickShapes give you twenty ready outlines, each with a fill, an outline and optional effects.

Drawing shapes and lines

To draw a shape or a line

  1. Choose the Rectangle, Ellipse or Line tool (or a QuickShape from Insert ▸ QuickShapes).
  2. Drag on the page to draw it. Hold Shift to constrain a perfect square or circle.
  3. Switch to the Pointer to move, resize or recolour it.

A full-width filled rectangle makes the coloured band behind a header or hero — the teal band on the sample home page is exactly that.

The QuickShape catalogue

QuickShapes are ready-made outlines. Pick one from the tool palette's Rectangle/Ellipse, or the rest from Insert ▸ QuickShapes, drag it out, then resize and recolour it like any other shape.

They cover geometry (triangles, diamonds, polygons), stars, arrows and a chevron, and the expressive shapes — heart, lightning bolt, speech bubble and cloud.

Fills, outlines and dashes

Every shape has a fill and an outline, set from the Colour panel. Set the outline width to zero for a shape with no border at all — the usual choice for a coloured background band. A line can be made solid or dashed.

Drop shadow and glow

Filter effects lift an object off the page, and WEBcreator publishes them as real CSS filters so they appear on the live site too.

To add a drop shadow or a glow

  1. Select the shape (or picture, or text).
  2. Open the Effects dialog (Effects — Shadow & Glow).
  3. Tick Enable drop shadow and set its colour, blur, offset and strength — or tick Enable outer glow for a soft halo.
  4. Click OK.
Chapter 8

Colour, Gradients and Transparency

Colour ties a site together. WEBcreator offers solid colours, swatches you keep to hand, smooth gradient fills, a coordinated site palette, and adjustable transparency.

Applying colour

To colour an object

  1. Select it.
  2. Open the Colour panel and choose whether you are setting the fill, the outline or the text colour.
  3. Pick a colour with the sliders, or type a hex value like #2a7d6b, or click a saved swatch.

Swatches and the site palette

The Swatches panel keeps a palette of colours one click away, so a site stays consistent — save a colour you use often and reuse it everywhere rather than matching hex values by hand. When you start from a design template, its colour scheme fills the palette for you, so every heading, band and button already belongs to the same small, coordinated set.

Gradient fills

A gradient fades one colour smoothly into another across a shape — a sky behind a headline, a soft panel behind text.

To fill a shape with a gradient

  1. Select the shape.
  2. Open the Linear Gradient (or Radial Gradient) dialog.
  3. Choose a start and end colour, and for a linear gradient, an angle.
  4. Click OK. The gradient scales with the object as you resize it, and publishes as a CSS gradient.

Transparency

Transparency lets what is behind an object show through it. A half-transparent coloured rectangle laid over a photo makes a tint you can read white text on; a faint shape becomes a watermark. Set an object's transparency from the panel — from fully solid to barely there.

Chapter 9

Tables and HTML

Beyond free text, WEBcreator builds the structured pieces a real site needs: tables for data, and — for anything bespoke — a raw HTML fragment and your own site-wide CSS.

Tables

To insert a table

  1. Choose the Table tool (or Insert ▸ Table) and drag out its size.
  2. Double-click the table to open the Edit Table editor.
  3. Set the number of rows and columns, type into the cells, and give the header row its own fill.
  4. Click OK. Drag the table’s edges to resize it.

A table is ideal for a price list, an opening-hours grid, or a simple comparison.

HTML fragments

When you need something WEBcreator does not build in — a booking widget, a third-party map, a snippet from another service — drop in an HTML Code object and paste the code.

To add a block of custom HTML

  1. Choose the HTML Code tool and drag out a box.
  2. In Edit HTML Fragment, paste or type the HTML.
  3. Click OK. The fragment is published exactly as written, inside your layout.

Embeds: comments, sign-ups and forms

Insert ▸ Embed… is a shortcut to the most common third-party blocks — a comments thread, a newsletter sign-up, an external form — so you do not have to find the embed code yourself.

Custom CSS

For a site-wide tweak — a web font, a hover effect, a rule that applies to every page — add your own Custom CSS.

To add your own CSS

  1. Choose Insert ▸ Custom CSS… (it sits right after Insert ▸ HTML Code).
  2. Type or paste your CSS rules.
  3. Click OK. The rules are written into every published page’s stylesheet.
RememberCustom HTML and CSS are powerful but unchecked — a mistake can break a page’s layout. Preview after any change.
Part III
Building a Website
Chapter 10

The Web Objects

These are the objects that make a page a living website rather than a static picture: navigation bars, buttons, forms, search, share buttons, video, audio, maps and a self-building news feed. Each is placed like any object, then set up in its own editor.

An overview

All the web objects, shown together on one page:

You add each from the tool palette or the Insert menu, and most open an editor as soon as you place them so you can set them up straight away.

Navigation bars

A Navigation Bar lists the pages of your site as links — and it does it automatically, so adding or renaming a page updates every nav bar at once.

To add a navigation bar

  1. Choose the Navigation Bar tool and drag it across the top of the page (usually on a master page, so it appears on every page).
  2. Double-click it to open the Navigation Bar editor.
  3. Choose a style — pills, underline or plain — and whether it runs across (horizontal) or down (vertical).
  4. Set the font, size and accent colour, then click OK.
NoteA sub-page (a page nested under another in the Site panel) shows as a drop-down under its parent, so a deep site still gets a tidy menu.

Buttons

A Button is a styled call to action that links somewhere — “Get a quote”, “Buy now”, “Download”.

To add a button

  1. Choose the Button tool and drag out its size.
  2. Double-click it and type its words.
  3. Set its fill colour and corner radius from the panels, and give it a hyperlink (Insert ▸ Hyperlink) to a page, a URL, an email or a file.
TipThe Buy Me a Coffee button on the Insert toolbar drops a ready-made, palette-matched support button in one click.

Forms

A Form lets visitors send you an enquiry without revealing your email address to spammers.

To add a contact form

  1. Choose the Form tool and drag out its size.
  2. In the Edit Form editor, list the fields you want (one per line) — for example Name, Email, Message.
  3. Set the submit button text, then click OK.
NoteA form needs somewhere to send its answers once the site is live. WEBcreator publishes the form ready to wire up to a free form-handling service — see the troubleshooting appendix.

Search box

A Search Box lets a visitor find anything on your site.

To add a search box

  1. Choose the Search Box tool and drag it out.
  2. In the editor, choose a search provider — Google, Bing or DuckDuckGo — and whether it searches just this site or the whole web.
  3. Set the placeholder and button text, then click OK.
NoteFor a site-only search you need to have set your site’s web address in Site-wide SEO, so the search engine knows which site to look within.

Share buttons

Share Buttons are a row of one-click links that let a visitor post your page to social media.

To add share buttons

  1. Choose the Share Buttons tool and drag out a row.
  2. In the Share Buttons editor, tick the networks you want — Facebook, X, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, Bluesky, Reddit, Threads or Email.
  3. Choose the button style, then click OK.

Video and audio

Embed media that plays right inside the page:

  • YouTube and Vimeo — place the object and paste the video's link; the player appears on the page.
  • Audio — place a player and choose a sound file or paste a link; it plays with the browser's own audio controls.

Google Maps

A Google Map shows an interactive map with a pin on your location — and it needs no API key.

To add a map

  1. Choose the Google Map tool and drag out its size.
  2. In the Google Map editor, type an address or place name and a label for the pin.
  3. Set the zoom level, then click OK.

The News Feed

A News Feed builds itself: it lists the sub-pages of the page it sits on, newest first, each as a card that links to the full story. Add a news story simply by adding a page under the News page — the feed updates automatically.

To add a self-building news feed

  1. Make a News page, and add each story as a page nested under it in the Site panel.
  2. On the News page, choose the News Feed tool and drag out a column.
  3. In the News Feed editor, choose the source page and how many stories to show, and whether to show each story’s date and picture.
  4. Click OK. Every story appears as a card, newest first.
TipInsert ▸ News from a Link… can create a story page straight from a web article’s address — handy for a press or blog section.
Chapter 11

Pages, Masters and Site Structure

A website is a set of linked pages that share a look. This chapter covers adding and arranging pages in the Site panel, the master pages that carry anything meant to repeat, and the links and navigation that tie the whole site together.

The Site panel

Open the Site panel (the Site Structure button) to see every page as a tree. A page nested under another is a sub-page; this is how a navigation bar builds its drop-downs and how a News Feed finds its stories.

To add, remove and arrange pages

  1. Choose Insert ▸ Page… (or the add button on the Site panel) and give the new page a name.
  2. Drag a page in the tree to reorder it, or indent it under another to make it a sub-page.
  3. Double-click a page to open it; delete a selected page from the panel.

Page properties

Each page has its own Page Properties (double-click it in the Site panel, or Format ▸ Page Properties…): its title, the file name it publishes as, which master page it uses, its background colour, and whether it should appear in navigation bars. A story page can also carry a date, which the News Feed shows on its card.

Master pages

Anything that should appear on every page — a logo, a navigation bar, a footer — belongs on a master page. A master sits behind the ordinary pages that use it, so you build the header once and it shows on every page.

To put a header on every page

  1. Switch to editing the master page (from the Site panel).
  2. Place the logo, navigation bar and footer on the master.
  3. Return to an ordinary page: those items now show on it, and on every page that uses the master.
  4. To change the header later, edit the master once and every page updates.
TipBuilt a page and only then realised several items repeat? Arrange ▸ Move Repeated Objects to Master Page… finds them and lifts them onto the master for you.

Hyperlinks everywhere

A link can live on text, a button, a shape or a picture, and can point to:

  • another page in your site (so a rename never breaks the link);
  • a web address on another site;
  • an anchor further down the same page;
  • an email address (opens the visitor's mail program);
  • a file to download.

Select the object (or some text), choose Insert ▸ Hyperlink…, and pick the target.

An automatic site index

Insert ▸ Index Page drops in a tidy, grouped list of every page on the site, each a working link — a ready-made sitemap for visitors. It keeps itself up to date as you add pages.

Checking your links

Before you publish, make sure nothing points nowhere.

To check every link on the site

  1. Choose File ▸ Check Links….
  2. WEBcreator lists every link on every page and flags any that are broken — a deleted page, a mistyped address.
  3. Fix each one at its source, then re-check.
Chapter 12

Search Engines (SEO)

A beautiful site is no use if nobody finds it. SEO — search-engine optimisation — is the handful of details that help Google and others understand and list your pages. WEBcreator makes it a fill-in-the-blanks job, per page and site-wide, and can even do it for you.

This page's SEO

Every page can have its own search-engine details.

To set a page’s SEO

  1. Open the page, then choose SEO ▸ This Page’s SEO….
  2. Write a concise title (what shows in the search result) and a one-sentence description.
  3. Give it a focus keyword — the phrase you hope people search for.
  4. Optionally set a social preview image (the picture that appears when the page is shared), and click OK.
NoteThe dialog scores each field as you type — a title that is the right length, a description that mentions the keyword — so you can see at a glance whether a page is well described.

Site-wide SEO

Some details belong to the whole site, not one page.

To set the site-wide SEO

  1. Choose SEO ▸ Site-wide SEO….
  2. Set the site’s base web address (needed for sitemaps, social cards and site search).
  3. Set a default social image, a Twitter / X handle, and your organisation details for rich search listings.
  4. Click OK.

Auto-generating SEO

If filling in a title and description for every page sounds like a chore, let the program do it.

To fill in SEO for every page at once

  1. Choose SEO ▸ Auto-generate SEO for all pages….
  2. WEBcreator reads the text on each page and writes a sensible title, description and keywords from it.
  3. Review the result — it is a starting point you can refine — and publish.

What WEBcreator does automatically

Even with no effort from you, WEBcreator writes the technical SEO on publish: a <title> and meta description for each page, social-sharing (Open Graph and Twitter) tags, a sitemap.xml that lists your pages for search engines, and a robots.txt. Filling in the SEO dialogs simply replaces its guesses with your own, better words.

Part IV
Templates & Design
Chapter 13

The Template Library

WEBcreator opens with around 92 ready-made designs: our own Basic Templates, plus the full Theme Layouts, Pro Templates and Sample Sites catalogue in the tradition of WebPlus. This chapter is an illustrated sample of each group — pick the nearest fit and make it yours.

Starting from a template

The fastest way to a finished site is to start from a design template — a complete, multi-page site you make your own. In the Startup Assistant's Use Design Template section you pick a design, choose a colour scheme, untick any pages you do not need, and open it as an ordinary, fully editable site.

To build a site from a template

  1. In the Startup Assistant, choose Use Design Template.
  2. Pick a design from the tree — our own Basic Templates, or one of Serif’s catalogue.
  3. Choose a colour scheme, and untick any pages you do not want.
  4. Click Open Template. It opens as a complete site.
  5. Replace the placeholder words and pictures with your own, recolour anything, then publish.
RememberA template is just a normal site once it opens — nothing is locked. Change everything freely.

Chapter 14

Designing a Page

The tools are only half the job; the other half is using them well. This chapter distils the handful of principles that separate a page that looks designed from one that looks thrown together — the same instincts a Squarespace or a WebPlus user relies on.

Start with a grid

Before placing anything, decide on your columns and lay guides against them. Lining every object up to the same few vertical lines is the single biggest thing that makes a layout feel calm and intentional. Two or three columns suit most pages; a full-width band can break the grid deliberately for a hero or a footer.

Alignment and white space

Line things up, and give them room. Nothing should sit a few stray pixels off from its neighbour — select and Align. And resist filling every corner: generous space around a headline makes a page look confident, not empty. Crowding is what reads as amateur.

A limited palette and two fonts

Pick two or three colours and stick to them — the site palette from your template makes this effortless. Do the same with type: one font for headings, one for body, and vary size and weight rather than adding more fonts. Restraint looks professional; variety for its own sake looks noisy.

Hierarchy: lead the eye

Decide what a visitor should see first, second, third — and let the sizes say so. A big headline, a clear subhead, calm body text, one bright button for the thing you want them to do. A landing page has one loud message; a content page has a heading, then sections. If everything shouts, nothing is heard.

Design for the phone too

More than half of most sites' visitors are on a phone. Keep the important things near the top, make tap targets (buttons, links) big enough for a thumb, and preview on the Phone device before you publish. A responsive site handles most of this for you, but a quick look on a narrow screen always pays off.

Part V
Worked Projects
Chapter 15

Project: A Small-Business Site

This project builds the one-page business site you have seen throughout the guide, from a blank page to a published layout — putting the skills of Parts II and III to work in order.

Set up the page and header

To start the site

  1. In the Startup Assistant choose Start New Site, name it, and create it at 960 px wide.
  2. Switch to the master page and draw a white header band across the top; place the logo as artistic text and a navigation bar beside it.

Add the hero

Back on the home page, draw a full-width coloured band below the header, and over it place an artistic headline, a line of frame text, and a bright button for the main call to action.

Lay out the content

To add the content

  1. Add a section heading, then three text frames side by side for the three services.
  2. Draw a wide picture frame below them and drop in a photo.

Finish and publish

Add a dark footer band on the master with your contact details. Run a spell check (F7) and File ▸ Check Links…, preview on a phone, then Publish.

TipSave this as your own starting point: next client, open it, change the words, the photo and the palette, and you are most of the way there.
Chapter 16

Project: A Portfolio

A portfolio is about the work, not the words. This short project shows the gallery-led way of thinking, using the kind of layout the Folio template provides.

Let the images lead

Start from the Folio template (or a blank site). The home page is mostly pictures: a grid of lightbox images or a photo gallery, with just enough text to say who you are.

To build the portfolio home page

  1. Place a short artistic headline and a line or two of intro text.
  2. Lay a grid of lightbox images — each a thumbnail that opens full-size when clicked — or a single photo gallery that cycles through your best work.
  3. Add an About and a Contact page, and a form or an email button so people can reach you.
RememberResist captions on everything and long explanations. In a portfolio, the work speaks; your words should be few and confident.
Chapter 17

Project: A Community or Club Site

A community group's site lives or dies on being kept up to date. This project leans on the self-building News Feed so that adding news is as easy as adding a page.

Structure it for easy updates

Start from the Meadow template, or build the pages: Home, Our Groups, Events, Get Involved, and a News page.

To set up a self-updating news section

  1. In the Site panel, add each news item as a page nested under the News page.
  2. On the News page, place a News Feed pointing at itself — every story appears as a card, newest first.
  3. On the home page, place a second, shorter News Feed showing the latest two or three stories.
  4. From now on, posting news means adding a page — the feeds and navigation update themselves.
TipA Google Map on the Contact page and a form for enquiries are the two things visitors to a club site look for most — add both.
Part VI
Preview & Publish
Chapter 18

Previewing Your Site

Before you put a site online, look at it the way a visitor will — in a real browser, and at phone, tablet and desktop widths. WEBcreator previews without publishing, so you can catch a problem before anyone sees it.

Preview in a window

The quickest check is the in-app preview, which shows the real published page and lets you switch screen sizes.

To preview at different screen sizes

  1. Choose Preview ▸ Preview as Website / Phone / Tablet….
  2. Click Website, Tablet or Phone to see the page at that width; use Rotate to swap portrait and landscape.
  3. Click any link or button — the preview is live, so navigation works.

Preview in your browser

To see a page exactly as the world will, in your own browser: Preview ▸ Preview Page in Browser opens the current page, and Preview Site in Browser opens the whole site with working navigation. This is the final look-over before publishing.

Chapter 19

Publishing Your Site

Publishing turns your design into a folder of real web files, and then puts them online. WEBcreator writes the files for you and walks you through getting them onto the web — including routes that need no technical knowledge at all.

What publishing produces

When you publish, WEBcreator writes a complete, self-contained website folder: an HTML file for each page, the images and files it uses, the stylesheet, and the sitemap.xml and robots.txt search engines expect. These are ordinary web files that any host in the world can serve.

Publishing

To publish your site

  1. Choose Publish on the menu bar.
  2. Choose whether the site should be Static (fixed width) or Responsive (scales to fit any screen).
  3. Click Publish. WEBcreator writes the whole site to a folder for you — you do not have to pick folders or file names.
  4. It then offers to put the site online (see below).

Putting it online

Once the files are written, WEBcreator helps you get them onto the web. It cannot host the site for you — that needs your own account somewhere — but it explains each option in plain English and opens the right page for it.

  • Netlify Drop — the recommended, no-account route. You drag the published folder onto a web page and your site is live in seconds, with a free address.
  • GitHub Pages — if you use GitHub, WEBcreator can publish a site straight to a Pages repository and update it again on each publish.
NoteOnce a site has been put online by one of these routes, publishing again just updates the live site — WEBcreator remembers where it lives and shows a short “updated” confirmation.

Updating a live site

A website is never finished. When you change something, choose Publish again: WEBcreator rewrites the files and, for a site it has already put online, pushes the update straight to the live address and tells you how many pages changed. For a drag-and-drop host, you drag the refreshed folder across once more.

Importing an existing site

If you already have a site elsewhere, you can bring it in and keep working on it here. From the Startup Assistant's Import… menu, import a website folder, a single web page from its URL, or a Serif WebPlus publication (.wpp). WEBcreator turns each into an editable site; your original is never altered.

Chapter 23

Appendix D — Glossary

The web-design words used in this guide.

A–Z

Anchor
A named spot on a page that a link can jump straight to.
Artistic text
A single line of display type you scale freely; publishes as real web text.
Breadcrumb
A trail of links showing where a page sits in the site.
Frame
A box that holds text or a picture; you size the box and its contents independently.
Gradient
A smooth fade from one colour to another across a shape.
Hyperlink
A clickable link to a page, address, email or file.
Lightbox
A thumbnail that opens the full picture in an overlay when clicked.
Master page
A page behind the others whose content repeats on every page that uses it.
Navigation bar
A menu of your pages that updates itself as pages change.
News Feed
A block that builds a list of story cards from a page's sub-pages.
Object
Anything you place on a page — text, picture, shape, button, form…
Open Graph
The tags that control how a page looks when shared on social media.
QuickShape
A ready-made shape outline (star, arrow, speech bubble…).
Responsive
A layout that scales to fit any screen, from phone to desktop.
SEO
Search-engine optimisation — the details that help a site be found.
Sitemap
A list of a site's pages, for search engines (and sometimes visitors).
Sub-page
A page nested under another in the Site panel.
Swatch
A saved colour kept one click away.
Chapter 24

Appendix E — Troubleshooting

Quick answers to common snags.

Common questions

My navigation bar is empty or missing a page.
A page only appears in navigation if its Page Properties has it ticked to show, so check there; and the nav lists pages at its own level — sub-pages appear as drop-downs under their parent.
My contact form does not send anything.
A form needs a server-side handler to deliver its messages. Publish the site, then point the form at a free form service (the published HTML is ready for one); a purely local preview cannot send mail.
My site-search finds nothing.
Site-only search needs your site's web address set in SEO ▸ Site-wide SEO, so the search engine knows which site to look within. Set it, then re-publish.
A picture looks fuzzy on the live site.
The image is smaller than the frame you stretched it into. Use a larger original, or make the frame smaller.
The page looks fine on my screen but cramped on a phone.
Publish as Responsive, and preview on the Phone device. For a fixed-width site, the phone shows the full width and the visitor scrolls.
I can't select an object.
It may be locked (Arrange ▸ Lock / Unlock), on a master page (edit the master), or behind another object (bring it forward, or use the Layers panel).
My YouTube video shows a blank box in the editor.
The editor fetches the poster image in the background; it appears once fetched, and the real player always shows on the published page.
The app won't start on Linux.
Run the installer again from a terminal; it sets up its own private Python environment automatically if the system one is missing.
